sections.abstract: BACKGROUND: Practical resistance of Helicoverpa zea to Cry proteins has become widespread in the US, making Vip3Aa the only effective Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) protein for controlling this pest. Understanding the genetic basis of Vip3Aa resistance in H. zea is essential in sustaining the long-term efficacy of Vip3Aa. The objectives of this study were to characterize the inheritance of Vip3Aa resistance in four distinct field-derived H. zea strains (M1-RR, AC4-RR, R2-RR and R15-RR), and to test for shared genetic basis among these strains and a previously characterized Texas resistant strain (LT#70-RR). RESULTS: Maternal effects and sex linkage were absent, and the effective dominance level (D ML ) was 0.0 across Vip3Aa39 concentrations ranging from 1.0 to 31.6 ∼g cm -2 , in all H. zea resistant strains. Mendelian monogenic model tests indicated that Vip3Aa resistance in each of the four strains was controlled by a single gene. However, interstrain complementation tests indicated that three distinct genetic loci are involved in Vip3Aa resistance in the five resistant H. zea strains: one shared by M1-RR and LT#70-RR; another shared by R2-RR and R15-RR; and a distinct one for AC4-RR. CONCLUSION: Results of this study indicate that Vip3Aa resistance in all H. zea strains was controlled by a single, recessive and autosomal gene. However, there were three distinct genetic loci associated with Vip3Aa resistance in the five resistant H. zea strains. The information generated from this study is valuable for exploring mechanisms of Vip3Aa resistance, monitoring the evolution of Vip3Aa resistance, and devising effective strategies for managing Vip3Aa resistance in H. zea.
sections.introduction: Helicoverpa zea (Boddie) (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae), commonly known as the bollworm or corn earworm, is a destructive pest of many crops of economic importance. Transgenic crops producing proteins from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) have been extensively grown worldwide for control of lepidopteran and coleopteran insect pests, including H. zea. 1 Within the US, there has been a remarkable increase in the prevalence of transgenic Bt corn and Bt cotton. The percentage of corn producing Bt proteins relative to the total acreage has risen from 1.4 to 84% during 1996-2022, whereas the proportion for cotton has increased from 14.6 to 89%. 1 Similar to chemical insecticides, widespread adoption of Bt crops has placed strong selection pressures on target insect populations, resulting in the evolution of resistance to Bt proteins and threatening the sustainable use of this valuable resource. [2][3][4] Until now, 11 species of Lepidoptera and Coleoptera have evolved practical resistance to Bt crops containing Cry proteins in at least 26 cases over seven countries. 5 Currently in the US, there are three primary families of Bt proteins employed to control H. zea, which include two crystal insecticidal proteins (Cry1 and Cry2) and one vegetative insecticidal protein (Vip3Aa). 6 Field-evolved H. zea resistance to Cry1 and Cry2 proteins in pyramided Bt corn and cotton is widespread in the US, as evidenced by the increasing number of documented fields with greater than expected damage levels in Bt crops producing only Cry1/Cry2 proteins, [7][8][9][10][11][12][13] and the increasing frequency of Cry1 and Cry2 resistance alleles in field populations of H. zea. 14,15 Consequently, Vip3Aa is the only effective Bt protein in pyramided Bt crops for control of H. zea in these regions. Moreover, decreased susceptibility and augmented damage of H. zea to Vip3Aa corn and cotton in the US has been increasingly reported during 2016-2022, possibly providing an early warning sign of field-evolved resistance, but with no practical resistance at this time. [10][11][12][13]16 To delay insect resistance development, a high dose-refuge strategy has been recommended for planting Bt crops in the US. 17 This strategy assumes that insect resistance to Bt proteins is inherited as a functionally recessive trait such that both susceptible homozygotes (SS) and heterozygotes (RS) can be eliminated. 17 If resistance is nonrecessive and allows RS to survive, the high dose-refuge strategy is less effective. 18 Studies have shown that H. zea has inherent low susceptibility to Bt proteins and exhibits nonrecessive resistance against Cry1 and Cry2 proteins. [19][20][21][22][23][24][25] Owing to these concerns, understanding the genetic basis of Vip3Aa resistance is important for developing appropriate IRM strategies. In 2019, Yang et al. used an F 2 screening method to establish a Vip3Aa-resistant strain of H. zea from populations collected in Texas and found that Vip3Aa resistance in this strain was autosomal, recessive and monogenic. 26,27 Recent results indicate that reduced Vip3Aa binding to receptors in the midgut is a mechanism of resistance in this H. zea strain. 28 Subsequently, four additional Vip3Aa-resistant strains of H. zea were established through F 2 screening with field insects collected from Winnsboro and Alexandria in Louisiana, and Stoneville in Mississippi during 2019-2020. 29 The availability of these resistant strains offers a unique opportunity to study the genetic basis of Vip3Aa resistance in H. zea collected from different geographical locations across different years. The specific objectives of this study were to first characterize the inheritance of Vip3Aa resistance in these four H. zea strains derived from Louisiana and Mississippi populations, and then determine whether the same genetic locus is involved with resistance in the five Vip3Aa resistant strains of H. zea derived from four locations across three southern states. The bioassay results indicate that Vip3Aa resistance in all the resistant strains is functionally completely recessive, autosomal and controlled by a single gene. However, there are three distinct genetic loci involved in Vip3Aa resistance among the five resistant H. zea strains. Data generated from this study is critical for developing resistance monitoring programs and management strategies for delaying evolution of resistance to Vip3Aa in H. zea. ## Insect sources A susceptible strain of H. zea, CBW-BZ-SS (abbreviated as SS), obtained from a commercial source, Benzon Research Inc. (Carlisle, PA, USA), served as a comparator for the resistant strains. The SS strain has been documented to be susceptible to Cry1Ac, Cry2Ab2 and Vip3Aa proteins in diet-overlay bioassays. 23 Five Vip3Aa resistant strains of H. zea were established using F 2 screening methods with insect populations collected from different geographical locations in the southern US during 2019-2020. These five Vip3Aa resistant strains consisted of one strain CBW-TX-LT#70-RR (abbreviated as LT#70-RR) derived from Snook, TX in 2019, previously referred to as CEW-Vip-RR in Kerns et al. 28 ; one strain CBW-LA-M1-RR (abbreviated as M1-RR) originated from Alexandria, LA in 2019; one strain CBW-LA-AC4-RR (abbreviated as AC4-RR) derived from Winnsboro, LA in 2020; and strains CBW-MS-R2-RR (abbreviated as R2-RR) and CBW-MS-R15-RR (abbreviated as R15-RR) originated from collections in Stoneville, MS in 2020. 26,29 These five resistant strains have been documented to show between >588.0and 909.1-fold resistance to Vip3Aa protein in diet-overlay bioassays relative to the susceptible strain. 26,29 In addition, Vip3Aa resistance in LT#70-RR has been documented to be monogenic, autosomal and recessive. 27 Before the current study, all Vip3Aa resistant strains had been backcrossed with SS and re-selected for resistance at least three times with a discriminating Vip3Aa protein concentration of 10 μg cm -2 in diet-overlay bioassays. The backcrossed reselected resistant strains were used in this study. In order tro characterize the inheritance of Vip3Aa resistance in the M1-RR, AC4-RR, R2-RR, and R15-RR strains of H. zea, we first conducted reciprocal crosses between the parental resistant strain (M1-RR, AC4-RR, R2-RR or R15-RR) and SS to generate eight F 1 progenies to test for dominance and sex linkage. Then, we sib-mated each of the eight F 1 progenies to generate eight F 2 progenies and determine whether Vip3Aa resistance is controlled by a single gene in the resistant strains. Finally, we performed reciprocal backcrosses between each F 1 progeny and the corresponding parental resistant strain to generate a total of 16 backcross progenies to determine if Vip3Aa resistance is controlled by a single gene. Therefore, a total of 37 insect strains or progenies were tested in the inheritance study. In order to determine whether the genetic basis of Vip3Aa resistance in the five Vip3Aa resistant strains is the same, we used LT#70-RR as a reference to conduct interstrain complementation tests for allelism. In the complementation tests, when two resistant strains with recessive alleles at different loci are crossed, the susceptibility is recovered in their F 1 progeny. 30 However, if the recessive alleles are at the same locus, the F 1 progeny is expected to be the same as their parents because the F 1 individuals inherit resistance alleles at the same locus from both parents. In this study, we found that Vip3Aa resistance in all five resistant strains of H. zea was recessive (see Section 3), and no maternal effects or sex linkage of Vip3Aa resistance was present in any of these resistant strains (see Section 3). Consequently, progenies generated from the reciprocal crosses between any two resistant strains were pooled in the interstrain complementation tests. Reciprocal crosses were first conducted between LT#70-RR and each of the four resistant strains. If the genetic basis of Vip3Aa resistance in M1-RR, AC4-RR, R2-RR or R15-RR was the same as LT#70-RR, no additional tests were conducted. Otherwise, additional reciprocal crosses between resistant strains showing different genetic basis relative to LT#70-RR, were performed using the same procedures as mentioned above. ## Purified Vip3Aa protein The purified full-length Vip3Aa39 protein used in bioassays was produced in cultures of a recombinant Escherichia coli strain, as described elsewhere. 28 The soluble Vip3Aa39 protoxin was collected and purified by anion-exchange chromatography with an AKTA Pure system (GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA). Fractions with eluted Vip3Aa39 were identified using SDS-PAGE, pooled and then protein concentration determined using the Qubit protein assay kit (Invitrogen/ Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) before storage at -80 °C. The Vip3Aa39 protein has high homology with the Vip3Aa19 protein (94.9%) produced in Bt cotton and the Vip3Aa20 protein (94.8%) produced in Bt corn. 26 ## Diet-overlay bioassays In order to determine whether Vip3Aa resistance in H. zea resistant strains in M1-RR, AC4-RR, R2-RR and R15-RR is recessive and autosomal, diet-overlay bioassays were conducted evaluating the susceptibility to Vip3Aa of the resistant strains, SS, and reciprocal crosses between each parental resistant strain and SS, as described in Yang et al. 23,27 The Vip3Aa concentrations used in the bioassays ranged from 0.0316 to 100.0 μg cm -2 . For the remaining insect strains and progenies, only two Vip3Aa concentrations, 3.16 and 10.0 μg cm -2 were used in the bioassays. To conduct the bioassays, 0.8 mL liquid diet (Southland Product, Inc., Lake Village, AR, USA) was first dispensed into each well of 128-well bioassay trays (C-D International, Pitman, NJ, USA) using repeater pipettes. Once the diet had cooled and solidified, a constant volume of 40 μL Bt protein solution suspended in 0.1% Triton-X100 was overlaid onto the surface of the diet. One neonate (<24 h) was placed on the diet surface of each well once the protein solution was air-dried. Each combination of insect strain by Vip3Aa protein concentration was replicated four times with 16 larvae per replication. The bioassay trays were placed in an insect rearing room under the conditions of 26 ± 1 °C, 50% relative humidity and a 16 h:8 h, light:dark photoperiod. Larval survival and instar were recorded after 7 days. ## Data analysis Larval mortality was calculated as percentage mortality (%) = 100 × (number of dead larvae + number of surviving larvae that were still in the first instar/total number of insects assayed). Larval mortality at each concentration of Vip3Aa was corrected based on the mortality observed on the control diet using the method of Abbott. 31 Probit analysis was used to determine the median lethal concentration (LC 50 ) that caused 50% mortality and the corresponding 95% fiducial limit (FL). 32 The resistance ratio for an insect strain was calculated as its LC 50 value divided by the LC 50 of SS. In addition, larval mortality at each concentration of Vip3Aa was analyzed using a one-way ANOVA with insect strain or progeny as the main factor. 32 To meet the normality assumptions for an ANOVA test, original data on the percentage of larval mortality were transformed using arcsine (χ0.5). Treatment means were separated using Tukey's honestly significant difference (HSD) test at the ⊍ = 0.05 level. Maternal effects and sex-linkage of Vip3Aa resistance in H. zea were assessed by comparing the LC 50 values and mortality between the two F 1 reciprocal crosses. 33 A significant difference in LC 50 values or mortality between the two F 1 reciprocal crosses would indicate that the resistance is sex-linked; otherwise the resistance is considered autosomal. The dominance of resistance was determined by comparing the LC 50 values and mortality of the F 1 strains with that of SS, and the parental resistant strains. sections.results: # Diverse genetic basis of Vip3Aa resistance in five independent field-derived strains of Helicoverpa zea in the US Authors: Fei Yang; Graham P Head; Dawson D Kerns; Juan Luis; José C Santiago-González; David L Kerns; Department of Entomology Texas A&M University College Station Texas USA Year: 2024 DOI: 10.1002/ps.7988
sections.discussion: Through F 2 screening for H. zea resistance to Vip3Aa in 2019-2020, we successfully established five distinct Vip3Aa resistant strains from field populations collected from Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi. In a previous study, we characterized the inheritance of Vip3Aa resistance in our first Vip3Aa resistant H. zea strain derived from Texas in 2019. 27 Here, we characterized the inheritance of Vip3Aa resistance in the remaining four H. zea strains from Louisiana and Mississippi. The results show that Vip3Aa resistance in each of the five H. zea strains collected from different locations in the southern US in different years is controlled by a single, recessive and autosomal gene. In another study, Carrière et al. reported that a laboratory-selected Vip3Aa resistant strain of H. zea displayed autosomal and almost completely recessive resistance to Vip3Aa protein. 37 These results suggest that autosomal recessive inheritance of Vip3Aa resistance may be a common occurrence in H. zea populations, which has significant implications for insect resistance management (IRM). The current highdose refuge IRM strategy for Bt crops relies on the assumption that resistance to Bt proteins in target insects is recessive, resulting in elimination of heterozygotes by high-dose Bt plants, thereby delaying the evolution of insect resistance to Bt crops. 17,38,39 Gene-pyramiding as another main IRM strategy for 6 Collectively, these findings suggest that both high-dose refuge and gene-pyramiding strategies should be effective in managing Vip3Aa resistance in H. zea, contingent upon meeting additional conditions such as ensuring abundant refuge plants and a rare initial resistance allele frequency. However, it is important to acknowledge that resistance to Cry1 and Cry2 is currently widespread in H. zea across US corn and cotton fields. [7][8][9]12,13 As Vip3Aa resistance evolves within this context, the complete efficacy of pyramiding Vip3Aa with Cry1 and/or Cry2 proteins for controlling H. zea resistance in the US might face limitations. In addition to H. zea, the genetic basis of Vip3Aa resistance has been explored in other lepidopteran insect pests. In Spodoptera frugiperda, for instance, resistance to Vip3Aa was monogenic, autosomal and recessive in both Brazilian and US populations established via F 2 screening. [42][43][44][45] Jin et al. also reported that a laboratory-selected Vip3Aa resistant strain of S. frugiperda in China showed autosomal and partially recessive resistance with a degree of dominance, h, of 0.13 (h = 0 indicates completely recessive resistance, h = 1 indicates completely dominant resistance). 46 However, this degree of dominance in S. frugiperda calculated by Jin et al. 46 was based on a Vip3Aa concentration of 0.4 μg cm -2 , which is lower than the concentration typically produced by Bt corn and cotton plants. [47][48][49][50] Previous studies show that the degree of dominance varies based on Bt concentrations, with nonrecessive resistance at low concentration and more recessive resistance at high concentrations. 23,51 Resistance to Vip3Aa in strains of Helicoverpa punctigera and Helicoverpa armigera from Australia also was monogenic and essentially recessive. 52,53 Our recent studies on Vip3Aa resistance in two Chloridea virescens strains established from F 2 screening with insects collected in Texas in 2021-2022 revealed that Vip3Aa resistance in those two strains is monogenic, autosomal and recessive (Santiago-González et al., unpublished data). By contrast, in another study on C. virescens resistance to Vip3Aa in a laboratory-selected strain with insects collected from the US, resistance to Vip3Aa was polygenic, and ranged from completely recessive to incompletely dominant. 36 These diverse outcomes suggest that the genetic basis of Vip3Aa resistance in a target insect pest may vary based on the methodologies used to establish resistant strains. Nevertheless, these published studies collectively suggest that Vip3Aa resistance in these lepidopteran insects tends to be autosomal and recessive, especially for strains derived from F 2 screening. Comprehending diversity in the genetic basis of Bt resistance across populations of a target insect pest is crucial for effective resistance monitoring and management programs. Current resistance monitoring efforts for H. zea in the US heavily rely on sentinel plots and F 2 screening, entailing substantial labor and materials. Alternatively, DNA-based resistance monitoring tools, based on whole genome 54,55 and targeted 56 sequencing, hold promise for enhanced sensitivity while concurrently reducing labor and material costs. If a single mutation governs Bt resistance across insect populations, molecular detection or targeted sequencing for that allele can effectively monitor and determine resistance frequency in the field. [56][57][58][59] Targeted sequencing can be easily adopted to detect multiple resistance alleles in cases where resistance entails multiple mutations, however, a list of candidate resistance genes is needed. Additionally, whole genome analyses can identify genetic variation associated with resistance emergence. 55 However, the only available study supporting applicability of whole genome analysis to identify and detect resistance alleles relied on a comparative analyses of insect samples collected over a period of 15 years. 55 Results from the present study support the existence of at least three distinct genetic loci for Vip3Aa resistance among five resistant H. zea strains: one shared by M1-RR and LT#70-RR; another shared by R2-RR and R15-RR; and a distinct one for AC4-RR. Interestingly, we did not detect temporal or geographical patterns in the genetic basis of resistance. For example, resistance in the M1-RR strain collected from Alexandria (LA) in 2019 and the strain LT#70-RR collected from Snook, TX in the same year localized to the same genetic locus. However, the M1-RR strain displayed a distinct genetic basis compared to the AC4-RR strain collected in Winnsboro (LA) in 2020, even though both strains were collected from Louisiana. The factors driving the diverse genetic basis of Vip3Aa resistance in H. zea across different years in different southern states remain unidentified. By contrast, it is not surprising that a shared genetic basis of Vip3Aa resistance was present between R2-RR and R15-RR, as both strains were derived from the same field collection in Stoneville (MS) in 2020. Considering the intense selection pressure in recent years for resistance to Vip3Aa in H. zea and the higher than expected Vip3Aa resistance allele frequency estimated from F 2 screening in only three southern states over 2019-2020, it's conceivable that there may be additional distinct genetic bases of Vip3Aa resistance in H. zea across US locations. Conducting further F 2 screening encompassing various locations and years is imperative to gain a better understanding of Vip3Aa resistance in this significant insect pest. Moreover, inheritance data provide valuable information to explore mechanisms and identify genes involved in resistance to Vip3Aa, advancing DNA-based approaches to monitor evolution of Vip3Aa resistance, and devising effective strategies for managing Vip3Aa resistance in H. zea. Recent work suggests that resistance in the LT#70-RR strain is associated with reduced Vip3Aa binding in the midgut of resistant larvae. 28 Current work is focused on determining if a similar mechanism explains resistance to Vip3Aa in the other available H. zea strains.
